narration.text: Let's build a coordinate grid — the stage where linear algebra plays out.
Now the unit circle. Every point on this circle is exactly one unit from the origin.
Here is our matrix A — a two-by-two grid of numbers. It encodes a transformation.
The equation A v equals lambda v is the eigenvalue equation. It asks: which vectors only get scaled?
Watch what happens when we multiply every point by A. The circle warps into an ellipse.
The grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced — that's what makes this a linear transformation.
But look — some directions got stretched more than others.
These special directions are the eigenvectors. They didn't rotate — they only scaled.
The first eigenvector scaled by about 2.46 — that's its eigenvalue, lambda one.
The second eigenvector scaled by about 1.04 — eigenvalue lambda two.
Let's rewind and watch again. Focus on the eigenvector — it stays on its line.
Now follow the second eigenvector. Same thing — it only stretches, never rotates.
That's what eigenvalues and eigenvectors really are — the DNA of a matrix transformation.
Every matrix has a story. Eigenvectors tell you the directions. Eigenvalues tell you how much.
